lessons.title: Add an order in cents
lessons.goal: Calculate a fictional lunch total without losing cents.
lessons.explanation: An int stores whole cents. decimal handles the fractional tax calculation; rounding converts it back to cents. The m suffix makes a decimal literal. checked makes an arithmetic overflow fail visibly. The sample uses a fictional 7.5% tax and a stated rounding rule, not tax advice or a complete checkout implementation.
steps: Read the Check calls before reading Quote. Predict the total on paper.
Trace 1,299 cents times 2, then round the sample tax once and add the 400-cent tip.
Download the C# project and run dotnet run locally. Match the output below.
Change AwayFromZero to ToEven. Run again and use the failing half-cent check to find the difference.
Restore the rounding rule, rerun, and record why the boundary case matters.
lessons.notebook:
Prediction: 1299 × 2 = ____ cents.
Tax: 2598 × 750 / 10000 = ____ cents before rounding.
Total including 400-cent tip: ____ cents.
Bug observed:
Fix and evidence:
lessons.expected:
Subtotal: 2598 cents
Tax: 195 cents; tip: 400 cents
Total: 3193 cents
PASS: money
lessons.challenge: Add a check that Quote(200, 3, 0, 50).Total is 650. Then add a delivery-fee parameter and a separate check for its effect. State whether your fictional tax includes that fee.

lessons.title: Stop an invalid order early
lessons.goal: Turn simple input rules into understandable validation messages.
lessons.explanation: A method accepts inputs and returns a list of problems. string? means the name may be null. Trimming removes surrounding spaces before checking the sample name. The quantity rule includes both endpoints: 1 and 20. These are exercise rules, not all of the application’s validation rules.
steps: Write down which cases should pass: quantity 0, 1, 20, and 21.
Read Validate and connect each if statement to its message.
Run the downloaded C# project locally and confirm all boundary checks pass.
Change quantity < 1 to quantity < 0. Rerun and read the zero-quantity failure.
Restore the rule and add your own check before extending validation.
lessons.notebook:
Rule in plain English:
Accepted boundary values:
Rejected boundary values:
What happened with a blank name?
Bug, fix, and passing evidence:
lessons.expected:
Enter a name from 1 to 40 characters.
Choose 1 to 20 items.
PASS: validation
lessons.challenge: Add a check for exactly 40 name characters. Then reject control characters such as a newline with a new message and a matching check.

lessons.title: Change a copy, keep the original
lessons.goal: Use a C# record to describe a menu item and make a changed copy.
lessons.explanation: A record groups named values and compares those values for equality. A with expression creates a copy with selected properties changed. The source record remains unchanged. This lesson uses only strings, integers, and booleans; with copies are shallow, so records containing mutable collections need more care.
steps: Identify each value in the MenuItem record at the bottom of the file.
Predict which values change in weekend and which stay the same.
Run locally and confirm the original menu item still costs 900 cents.
Change the weekend price to 900. Rerun and use the price check to locate the bug.
Restore the price, then create a separate unavailable copy.
lessons.notebook:
Original values:
Copied values:
Why are sameValues and original equal?
What does with leave unchanged?
Bug and evidence:
lessons.expected:
Original: Garden soup, 900 cents
Weekend: Garden soup, 950 cents
Sold-out copy available: False
PASS: records
lessons.challenge: Make a renamed copy and verify that its name changes while the original name and price stay unchanged. Explain why a copied menu item would still need validation before saving.

lessons.title: Keep each restaurant’s orders separate
lessons.goal: Look up an order using both a restaurant identifier and an order identifier.
lessons.explanation: A tenant is one restaurant or business in a shared application. An order number alone may appear in several restaurants. The lookup must match both values. This is a data-filtering exercise, not authentication or authorization: real server code must first establish which tenant the signed-in person may access.
steps: Notice that both fictional restaurants have an order named order-1.
Trace the two comparisons in FindOrder and predict each result.
Run locally. Confirm that an unknown restaurant receives no order.
Remove o.TenantId == tenantId && from the lookup. Run again to see the isolation check fail.
Restore the tenant comparison and write why a browser-supplied tenant alone is insufficient.
lessons.notebook:
Tenant means:
Why can order-1 exist twice?
What must the lookup match?
What would a real server need to authorize first?
Bug and evidence:
lessons.expected:
Lantern order: 1200 cents
Harbor order: 900 cents
PASS: tenants
lessons.challenge: Add a third restaurant with order-1 and a different total. Write a check proving its result is separate, and another proving a missing order is not replaced by a different restaurant’s order.

lessons.title: Retry without a second order
lessons.goal: Reuse a receipt for an identical repeated request and reject conflicting reuse.
lessons.explanation: A request key names one attempt to create an order. Repeating the same tenant, key, and payload returns the original receipt. Reusing that key with changed details fails. The in-memory dictionary demonstrates the idea only: production needs durable storage, transactions, uniqueness constraints, concurrency handling, and review before retrying side effects.
steps: Find the dictionary key: it combines Tenant and Key.
Predict how many stored orders remain after an identical retry.
Run locally and confirm the retry returns the same receipt and a conflict adds nothing.
Change request with { Quantity = 2 } to request. Run again; the conflict check should fail because you no longer submitted changed details.
Restore the changed payload. Explain why a new request key would create a new order.
lessons.notebook:
What identifies one attempted order?
What is returned after an identical retry?
What happens when its payload changes?
Why is an in-memory dictionary insufficient in production?
Bug and evidence:
lessons.expected:
First receipt: order-1
Retry receipt: order-1
Stored orders: 2
PASS: retries
lessons.challenge: Submit the same item with attempt-2 for Lantern Cafe. Add checks that a new receipt is created and there are now three orders. Then explain why changing the key is not a safe response to every uncertain result.
